new_statements.quote: [p.23] Dimasa is a tonal language with three register tones- high, mid and low. The sentence constructions end in falling intonation in the language with mostly trochaic word accents. This is a typical suprasegmental feature of the Bodo-Garo languages which share similar features with some of the Austro-Asiatic languages. [p.88] All the dialects of Dimasa are tonal with some intonation only in polysyllables and sentences. Stress (primary) and accent (low and high) function only to distinguish different dialects in Dimasa. [p.89] Longer words, which are polysyllabic, carry lexical intonation in each syllable while tone is marked at the final syllable in Dimasa.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dimasa is described as a register-tone language (H, M, L) in which stress/accent is not lexically contrastive ('functions only to distinguish dialects'); word accent is characterised in passing as 'mostly trochaic' (i.e. word-initial prominence in disyllables), while the single lexical tone of a word is realised on its final syllable. No fuller rule (syllable counting, weight) is given anywhere in the accessible literature.
new_statements.exceptions: 'mostly' trochaic (no exceptions listed); stress/accent said to vary between dialects (Hasao standard vs Hawar, Dembra, Dijuwa) without detail. Note the tension with other descriptions: Sarmah 2009 finds initial syllables of disyllables short (70 vs 120 ms) with lexical tone only on the final syllable, and Jacquesson 2008 / Evans & Langthasa 2024 describe weak, reducible first syllables (sesquisyllables) -- all pointing to final-syllable prominence rather than trochaic accent; none of them uses the word 'stress'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level typological remark (citation forms); the p.88 passage is in the intonation section and concerns dialect differentiation. Variety: Standard Hasao dialect (Haflong, Dima Hasao).
new_statements.identity_note: Longmailai 2014 describes the Standard Hasao dialect (Haflong, Dima Hasao district), the variety declared standard by the Dimasa Sahitya Sabha; Evans & Langthasa 2024 also Haflong; Rajioung 2021/2025 cover Hawar (Cachar), Dembra and Dijuwa dialects. All fall under glottocode dima1251 (no separate dialect glottocodes used). Longmailai states stress/accent differs between dialects.

sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: No stress statement. Every prosodic word carries exactly one lexical tone, on the rightmost syllable; initial syllables of disyllables get a default mid tone and are much shorter (70 ms vs 120 ms, Table 4-2, p.80); suffixes toneless.

sources.citation: Jacquesson, Francois. 2008. A Dimasa Grammar. Unpublished ms., 62 pp. (Brahmaputra Studies Database, CNRS; Wayback copy).
sources.note: No stress statement. 'A sketch of phonology' pp.9-15: two tones (higher marked with superscript 2), weak/dropped vowels in first syllables (bV-, gV-, sV-, pV- prefixes). Only prosodic remark: bare imperative 'marked of course by contour, usually with a rising pitch and louder voise on the end of the word' (sec.2.2.3.2.1).

sources.citation: Evans, Jonathan P. & Dhrubajit Langthasa. 2024. Dimasa Language: Structure and Texts. Language and Linguistics Monograph Series 66. Taipei: Institute of Linguistics, Academia Sinica. 270 pp. (open access)
sources.note: Silent on word stress (the word 'stress' does not occur in the phonology chapter, pp.3-22). Describes sesquisyllables /CvCV(C)/ with a light first syllable whose vowel echoes the main vowel; sec.2.4: Haflong variety gives no convincing evidence for tones, though other descriptions report 2-3 tones realized on final syllables.

sources.note: Supra-segmental section = two register tones (high, low). No stress statement. Cites Burling 2007 'Dimasa Tones' unpublished ms.
